**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,

$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$

For $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ with $\mu\ge0$ and integer $K\ge0$, write $\tau_K(\mu):=\mathbb P(N>K)$. If $\mu=0$, then $\tau_K(\mu)=0$. If $\mu>0$ and $\mu<K+2$, then

$$\tau_K(\mu)\le \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}.$$

The right side is a geometric majorant computed from a Poisson mass, not a floating-point subtraction of a rounded partial sum from one.

$$G_K(\mu):=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}\le\varepsilon/m.$$

$$v_{k+1}=Pv_k,\qquad w_{k+1}=w_k\frac{\mu}{k+1},\qquad x_j\leftarrow x_j+w_{k+1}v_{k+1}.$$

These $P$ actions use the exact operator-application interface of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]]: the routine supplies $v\mapsto Pv$ and vector additions and scalar multiples, without requiring stored matrix entries. No CSR representation, operation-count estimate, or convergence claim is part of this procedure. The exact term count is $m(K+1)\le B$ and the certified tail bound satisfies $T\le\varepsilon$. For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

derivations.claim: For any $\mu>0$, set $S_\mu=e^{\mu Q/\nu}=e^{-\mu}e^{\mu P}$ and $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)P^k$. By [F1], each $P^k$ is nonnegative and column stochastic; [F2] and [F3] give $S_\mu=\sum_{k\ge0}w_k(\mu)P^k$ with nonnegative weights summing to one. Thus $R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $s_K:=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)\le1$, and $S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $\tau_K(\mu)$.

The induced norm formula [F6] gives $\|S_\mu\|_1=1$, $\|R_{\mu,K}\|_1=s_K$, and $\|S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}\|_1=\tau_K(\mu)$. If $\lambda=\nu t=0$, only the $k=0$ Poisson weight is nonzero, so $p(t)=u_K(t)=p_0$ and the omitted mass is zero. If $\lambda>0$, apply step 1.1 with $\mu=\lambda$: $(S_\lambda-R_{\lambda,K})p_0$ is nonnegative and its coordinate sum is $\tau_K(\lambda)$; by [F5], the exact one-series $\ell^1$ omitted mass is therefore exactly the scalar Poisson tail.

In the time-split algorithm, $0<\mu\le1$ and $K\ge0$, so $\mu<K+2$ and [F4] gives $\tau_K(\mu)\le G_K(\mu)$. For $m$ substeps the telescoping identity $S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}S_\mu^{m-1-j}(S_\mu-R_{\mu,K})R_{\mu,K}^j$, [F5]–[F6], and step 2.1 give $\|S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m\|_1\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu)$.

Every term in the telescoping identity is nonnegative, so the exact vector error on $p_0$ is nonnegative. Each column sum of $S_\mu^m$ is one and each column sum of $R_{\mu,K}^m$ is $s_K^m$; hence its $\ell^1$ mass is exactly $1-s_K^m=1-(1-\tau_K(\mu))^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)$. This proves the exact time-split lost-mass identity and the preceding error bound.

Since $m\mu=\nu t$, [F8] gives $S_\mu^m=e^{tQ}$ and [F2] gives $S_\mu^mp_0=p(t)$, while [F7] identifies the exact truncated output as $R_{\mu,K}^mp_0$. The triangle inequality for the vector $1$-norm [F5] therefore yields $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le\|p(t)-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1+\|R_{\mu,K}^mp_0-\widehat u\|_1\le mG_K(\mu)+E_{\rm alg}\le T+E_{\rm alg}$ when the validated upper bound $T$ is supplied. If $\nu t=0$, the algorithm returns $p_0$ and both error terms are zero.

Let $S$ be a nonempty at most countable state space, and let $q(x,y)\ge0$ be a finite transition rate for each pair $x,y\in S$ with $x\ne y$. Require the total exit rate

$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$$

to be finite for every $x$. The associated **column rate matrix convention** is $Q_{yx}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ and $Q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$; thus the source state indexes the column. No finite-dimensional matrix is asserted for an infinite $S$.

A **given time-homogeneous pure-jump Markov chain with rates $q$** is a process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with values in $S$ whose conditional future law given its history depends only on its present state and elapsed time, and whose paths are constant between successive jumps. Its transition kernels $K_t$ depend only on elapsed time, satisfy $K_0=I$, and obey $K_{s+t}=K_sK_t$ using the composition $(K_sK_t)(x,A):=\int_S K_t(z,A)\,K_s(x,dz)$ of [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]]. At state $x$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, its holding time has survival $e^{-\lambda(x)t}$ and its next state is $y\ne x$ with probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$, independently of that holding time; at $\lambda(x)=0$ it stays at $x$. It is **nonexplosive** when almost surely it has only finitely many state changes on every bounded time interval.

The chain and nonexplosion are input hypotheses in this item and in the projection results below. This definition does not construct a chain from an arbitrary countable rate matrix and proves no general nonexplosion claim.

Let $X$ be a given nonexplosive chain as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]], with initial law $p_0$ on $S$, and let $F\subseteq S$ be finite and nonempty. Its first exit time from $F$ is

$$\tau_F:=\inf\{s\ge0:X_s\notin F\},$$

with $\tau_F=0$ when $X_0\notin F$. Adjoin a new state $\dagger\notin S$ and define the **killed projection** $Y_t=X_t$ for $t<\tau_F$ and $Y_t=\dagger$ for $t\ge\tau_F$. The **killed mass vector** is $u_F(t,x):=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$, and the **cemetery mass** is $c_F(t):=\mathbb P(Y_t=\dagger)$. Initially, $u_F(0,x)=p_0(x)$ for $x\in F$ and $c_F(0)=p_0(S\setminus F)$.

For $x\in F$ let $\lambda(x)=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$. The killed principal subgenerator on $F$ has entries $(Q_F)_{y x}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ in $F$ and $(Q_F)_{x x}=-\lambda(x)$; its column sum is $-\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. The **cemetery lift** is the finite matrix $\widetilde Q_F$ on $F\cup\{\dagger\}$ with these same entries on $F$, with

$$\widetilde Q_{\dagger x}=\lambda(x)-\sum_{\substack{y\in F\\y\ne x}}q(x,y)=\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{x\dagger}=0\quad(x\in F),\qquad \widetilde Q_{\dagger\dagger}=0.$$

Every column of $\widetilde Q_F$ sums to zero and its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, so it is a finite column generator in the sense of [[def-xd-finite-column-generator]]. The cemetery state is absorbing; trajectories that return to $F$ after their first exit remain at $\dagger$ in this projection.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

Let $S$ be at most countable. For nonnegative functions $a,b:S\to[0,\infty)$ with finite total masses, define

$$\|a-b\|_{\ell^1(S)}:=\sum_{x\in S}|a(x)-b(x)|.$$

For a nonnegative family, $\sum_{x\in S}$ means the supremum of its finite subsums; this agrees with the ordinary series under any enumeration of $S$. The distance is finite because $|a(x)-b(x)|\le a(x)+b(x)$ termwise, so $\|a-b\|_{\ell^1(S)}\le\sum_xa(x)+\sum_xb(x)$. In particular it is defined for probability and subprobability mass functions.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: For each source state $x\in F$, the off-diagonal entries of $\widetilde Q_F$ are the internal rates $q(x,y)$ and the exit rate to $\dagger$ is $\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. Their sum is $\lambda(x)$, so the diagonal $-\lambda(x)$ makes the column sum zero. The cemetery column is zero. Therefore $\widetilde Q_F$ is a finite column generator.

By the definition of $Y$, for each $x\in F$ the event $\{Y_t=x\}$ is exactly $\{X_t=x,\tau_F>t\}$; the complementary event $\{Y_t=\dagger\}$ is $\{\tau_F\le t\}$. Therefore $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x)$ and $c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)$. Returning paths are included in $p_t$ but excluded from $u_F$ by the strict first-exit condition.

Let $M_F=\max_{x\in F}\lambda(x)$, finite because $F$ is finite. For $0\le h\le1$, [F6] bounds the exponential series remainder by $|e^{-\lambda(x)h}-(1-\lambda(x)h)|\le h^2\sum_{k\ge2}\lambda(x)^k/k!$, so no-jump probability is $1-\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ uniformly on finite $F$. If $\lambda(x)>0$, the first-jump probability $1-e^{-\lambda(x)h}=\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ multiplied by the destination probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$ from [F1] gives rate $q(x,y)h+o(h)$ for each $y\ne x$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, all rates from $x$ are zero and these probabilities are zero. For the aggregate exit event, its conditional destination probability is $a_x/\lambda(x)$ when $\lambda(x)>0$, so its probability is $a_xh+o(h)$; when $\lambda(x)=0$, $a_x=0$ and this probability is zero. Here $a_x=\lambda(x)-\sum_{y\in F,y\ne x}q(x,y)\ge0$. After reaching $\dagger$ there are no further changes. By [F5] applied to $-u$, $1-e^{-u}\le u$ for $u\ge0$, so the probability of a first change within $h$ is at most $M_Fh$; conditional on a first change that stays in $F$, a second change within the remaining time has probability at most $M_Fh$. Hence the probability of two or more changes is at most $M_F^2h^2$. Thus the finite transition matrix of $Y$ is $I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ as $h\downarrow0$, uniformly over its finite state space.

Extend $u_F$ by zero outside $F$. For $x\in F$, $p_t(x)-u_F(t,x)\ge0$ by step 1.2; for $x\notin F$, the difference is $p_t(x)\ge0$. Summing these nonnegative differences over $S$ gives $1-\sum_{x\in F}u_F(t,x)=1-\mathbb P(\tau_F>t)=c_F(t)$. By [F4], this sum is exactly $\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}$.

The process $Y$ is Markov: before killing this follows from the Markov property of $X$, and after killing its state $\dagger$ is absorbing. Hence its finite column transition matrix $T_Y(h)$ satisfies $T_Y(h)=I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ entrywise by step 2.1, and its law satisfies $\widetilde p(t+h)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t)$. This gives the right derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$. For $t>0$, $\widetilde p(t)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t-h)$. Since the state space has finitely many coordinates, the entrywise expansion and $\sum_j\widetilde p_j(t-h)=1$ imply each coordinate of $\widetilde p(t)-\widetilde p(t-h)$ is $O(h)$; hence $\widetilde p(t-h)\to\widetilde p(t)$. Dividing the identity by $h$ and using the entrywise limit $(T_Y(h)-I)/h\to\widetilde Q_F$ gives the left derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$ as well, because every coordinate is a finite sum. Thus $\widetilde p'=\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p$ with initial law $\widetilde p(0)$. By [F3], $\widetilde p(t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\widetilde p(0)$.

Let $a=\inf f$, $b=\sup f$, and $c=(a+b)/2=f(\dagger)$. The coupling uses the same path $X$: on $\{\tau_F>t\}$, $Y_t=X_t$, and on $\{\tau_F\le t\}$, $Y_t=\dagger$. Thus $|\mathbb E f(X_t)-\mathbb E f(Y_t)|=|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{\tau_F\le t\}}(f(X_t)-c)]|\le\tfrac12(b-a)\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)=\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t)$, as asserted.

**Inputs.** A given nonexplosive chain $X$ and initial law $p_0$; a finite positive integer $N$ and an explicitly supplied nested list of nonempty finite sets $F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_N$; for each $F_i$, its exact finite cemetery-lift generator $\widetilde Q_{F_i}$ and lifted initial vector from [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]; final time $T\ge0$; tolerance $\varepsilon>0$; and a positive integer per-projection term cap $B$.

The supplied lift data must be the exact rates and initial masses of the given chain. An implementation may obtain the cemetery rate from the exact exit rate minus the finite sum of within-$F_i$ rates. The arithmetic backend must enclose each computed cemetery coordinate and provide the certified arithmetic/algebraic error required by [[thm-xd-uniformization-truncation-and-error]].

**Procedure.** For $i=1,\ldots,N$ in order:

1. Apply [[alg-xd-budgeted-uniformization-accumulation]] to $(\widetilde Q_{F_i},\widetilde p_{F_i,0},T)$ with at most $B$ terms. If it returns `budget-exhausted`, `certificate-unavailable`, or the exact lift data are unavailable, return `inconclusive` with the statuses and all completed projection records; do not skip an uncertified projection.
2. Let $\widehat c_i$ be the computed cemetery coordinate and let $\delta_i$ be the total certified $\ell^1$ error bound (Poisson-tail plus arithmetic/algebraic error). Form the outward-certified interval
   $$L_i=\max(0,\widehat c_i-\delta_i),\qquad U_i=\min(1,\widehat c_i+\delta_i).$$
   Record $F_i$, the computed vector, $\widehat c_i$, $[L_i,U_i]$, its tail bound, and its arithmetic/algebraic error.
3. If validated interval arithmetic certifies $U_i\le\varepsilon$, return `certified` with this projection and its record.

If all $N$ projections have valid records but none passes the tolerance, return `inconclusive` with every record. The algorithm uses at most $N$ projections and $NB$ uniformization terms. It makes no claim that some finite projection outside this supplied list meets $\varepsilon$.

Let $X_t$ be a given nonexplosive countable chain with rates $q(x,y)$, initial law $p_0$, and finite exit rates as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]]. For a finite nonempty $F\subseteq S$, let $\tau_F$ and $Y_t$ be the killed projection of [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]. Write $p_t(x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x)$ and $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$. Then

$$u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x),\qquad c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t).$$

If $\bar u_F$ is $u_F$ extended by zero to $S\setminus F$, then

$$\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}=c_F(t).$$

For any bounded real observable $f:S\to\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{osc}(f):=\sup_{x\in S}f(x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)$ and extend it to the cemetery state by $f(\dagger):=(\sup f+\inf f)/2$. The corresponding expectation error obeys

$$|\mathbb E[f(X_t)]-\mathbb E[f(Y_t)]|\le\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t).$$

The finite cemetery lift $\widetilde Q_F$ in [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]] is a finite generator and $\mathcal L(Y_t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\mathcal L(Y_0)$. A path that exits $F$ and later returns contributes to the full marginal but remains at the cemetery state in the killed projection.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator, $p_0$ a column probability vector, and $\nu>0$ an admissible rate. For $\lambda=\nu t$ and $K\ge0$, the exact one-series partial sum

$$u_K(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}P^kp_0$$

is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact $\ell^1$ distance from $p(t)$ is the scalar Poisson tail $\tau_K(\lambda)=\mathbb P(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)>K)$. If $\nu t>0$, the budgeted algorithm sets $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m\le1$, and uses $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K e^{-\mu}\mu^kP^k/k!$. Then $R_{\mu,K}^m p_0$ is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact transient $\ell^1$ error is

$$1-\left(\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^k}{k!}\right)^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu).$$

If a computed vector $\widehat u$ has a separately certified accumulated arithmetic/algebraic error $E_{\rm alg}:=\|\widehat u-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le mG_K(\mu)+E_{\rm alg}$. In rounded arithmetic, if $T$ is a validated upper bound for $mG_K(\mu)$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. Fix positive integers $d$ and $R$. A **reaction propensity system** consists of a state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ that is finite or countable, increments $\nu_j\in\mathbb Z^d$ for $1\le j\le R$, and propensities $a_j:E\to[0,\infty)$. Here “countable” means finite or countably infinite, as in [[def-countable]]. The total propensity
$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$$
is finite for every $x\in E$, and $a_j(x)>0$ implies $x+\nu_j\in E$. Here $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbb Z$ have the meanings in [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-integers]], and addition in $\mathbb Z^d$ is coordinatewise.

A **reaction event** of channel $j$ at state $x$ records the marked transition $x\mapsto x+\nu_j$. The counting process $N_j(t)$ records the number of channel-$j$ events by time $t$. A zero increment $\nu_j=0$ is allowed: it records a reaction event without changing the state.

For a time-homogeneous system, the **reaction generator operator** on bounded functions $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is
$$(Qf)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0} a_j(x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
When $E$ is finite, $\Lambda:=\max_{x\in E}\lambda(x)<\infty$. If no active reaction has zero increment, the corresponding matrix has off-diagonal entries $q_{xy}=\sum_{j:x+\nu_j=y}a_j(x)$ and diagonal $q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$. With zero-increment events, the operator formula remains valid and the matrix diagonal is instead minus the sum of state-changing rates; the zero-increment channels remain part of the marked event process.

For a finite horizon $T$, a **time-dependent propensity system** replaces $a_j(x)$ by functions $a_j:[0,T]\times E\to[0,\infty)$ whose sections $t\mapsto a_j(t,x)$ are measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B([0,T])$ of the usual topology on $[0,T]$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Require finite total rate $\lambda(t,x):=\sum_j a_j(t,x)$. Its time-dependent generator operator is
$$(Q_t f)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(t,x)>0} a_j(t,x)\bigl(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x)\bigr).$$
This definition specifies a stochastic model. It does not assert that a physical chemical system follows that model.

For $V:E\to[1,\infty)$, call $V$ **proper** when $\{x:V(x)\le n\}$ is finite for every integer $n\ge1$. For this possibly unbounded $V$, define the finite local expression
$$(QV)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(V(x+\nu_j)-V(x)\bigr);$$
this does not assert that $V$ belongs to the bounded-function domain of the generator in [F1]. Suppose $QV\le cV$ for a constant $c\ge0$. Define $T_m$ as the time of the $m$th reaction event, with $T_m=\infty$ if fewer than $m$ events occur. Then the explosion time $\tau_\infty:=\lim_{m\to\infty}T_m$ satisfies $\mathbb P_{x_0}(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. No full Axiom of Choice is used.

$$\lambda(x):=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$$

to be finite for every $x$. The associated **column rate matrix convention** is $Q_{yx}=q(x,y)$ for $y\ne x$ and $Q_{xx}=-\lambda(x)$; thus the source state indexes the column. No finite-dimensional matrix is asserted for an infinite $S$.

A **given time-homogeneous pure-jump Markov chain with rates $q$** is a process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ with values in $S$ whose conditional future law given its history depends only on its present state and elapsed time, and whose paths are constant between successive jumps. Its transition kernels $K_t$ depend only on elapsed time, satisfy $K_0=I$, and obey $K_{s+t}=K_sK_t$ using the composition $(K_sK_t)(x,A):=\int_S K_t(z,A)\,K_s(x,dz)$ of [[def-composition-of-probability-kernels]]. At state $x$ with $\lambda(x)>0$, its holding time has survival $e^{-\lambda(x)t}$ and its next state is $y\ne x$ with probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$, independently of that holding time; at $\lambda(x)=0$ it stays at $x$. It is **nonexplosive** when almost surely it has only finitely many state changes on every bounded time interval.

The chain and nonexplosion are input hypotheses in this item and in the projection results below. This definition does not construct a chain from an arbitrary countable rate matrix and proves no general nonexplosion claim.

$$\tau_F:=\inf\{s\ge0:X_s\notin F\},$$
